title: How would you debug a page with poor INP?
description: Use Chrome DevTools and React Profiler to find long interactions, identify the responsible code, and improve Interaction to Next Paint.

data.text: INP (Interaction to Next Paint) measures how quickly a page responds to user input—clicks, taps, key presses. A poor INP means the main thread is busy when the user interacts. In React apps, the usual suspects are: large synchronous renders, expensive effects, long JavaScript tasks from third-party scripts, and layout thrashing. Debugging INP requires finding the **long task** that blocked the interaction.

INP is based on the latency of all interactions during a page session. Google recommends INP under 200ms. A page scores its INP from roughly the 98th percentile of interaction latencies. So one very slow interaction—like a button click that takes 500ms to respond—can tank your score even if most interactions are fast.

terms.definition: Interaction to Next Paint: a Core Web Vital measuring the latency of all interactions a user makes with a page.
Any JavaScript execution that blocks the main thread for more than 50ms.
The single thread where JavaScript runs in the browser. It handles rendering, event processing, and JS execution—all sequentially.
The time from when the user triggers an event (click) to when the browser paints the next frame. Includes event dispatch, React render, and layout/paint.

data.title: Chrome DevTools Performance panel
items: Open DevTools → Performance → check 'Screenshots' and 'Web Vitals'
Click Record, then interact with the page (click buttons, type, scroll)
Stop recording after 10-20 seconds of activity
Look for red bars labeled 'Long Task' in the Main thread track
Click a long task to see its call stack. Look for React, third-party scripts, or your own functions
If React is in the stack, open the React Profiler to identify which component took the most time

data.title: Why React apps have poor INP
items: A click handler triggers a state update that causes a large component subtree to re-render synchronously
A dropdown menu renders a long list without virtualization—creating hundreds of DOM nodes in one frame
`useEffect` with expensive synchronous work blocks the commit phase after the event
Third-party scripts (analytics, A/B testing, chat widgets) compete with React for main-thread time
Large JSON payloads parsed synchronously in the event handler

data.title: Expensive synchronous render on click
data.content: A button click sets state that causes a parent to re-render a large list. The render blocks the main thread for 200ms+.

data.title: Fix: virtualization + debounced filtering
data.content: Render only visible items with a virtualizer, and debounce the filter to avoid filtering on every keystroke.

data.text: The React Profiler measures **commit times**—how long React takes to apply changes to the DOM. A commit that takes 100ms will directly contribute to INP if it happens in response to a user event. Use the Profiler during the same interaction you profiled in the Performance panel to correlate the long task with a specific component render.

data.title: Focus on the 98th percentile
data.text: Lab tests on fast hardware won't reproduce slow INP. Use Chrome's throttling (6x CPU slowdown) or test on real mid-range mobile devices. CrUX data in Search Console shows your real-world INP distribution.

data.caption: Systematic approach to debugging poor INP

items: Virtualize long lists with `@tanstack/react-virtual` so only visible items render
Wrap expensive event handlers in `requestIdleCallback` or break work into chunks with `setTimeout(0)`
Use React Compiler (React 19) or manual `useMemo` to avoid redundant work
Defer third-party scripts with `async` or `defer`, or load them after interaction
Use `scheduler.yield()` or `startTransition` to break large renders into smaller, interruptible units

items.question: What's the difference between INP and FID?
items.answer: FID (First Input Delay) measured only the first interaction's delay. INP replaces it and measures the **worst** interaction latency across the entire page session. A page could have a fast first click but a slow save action later—FID wouldn't catch it; INP does.

items.question: Does React 19's automatic memoization help with INP?
items.answer: Yes. The React Compiler automatically memoizes components and hooks, reducing unnecessary re-renders that contribute to long commit times. It's one of the most impactful React 19 features for INP, but you should still profile—the compiler can't fix expensive logic inside render.

items.question: Can Web Workers help with INP?
items.answer: Web Workers move computation off the main thread, which helps for heavy data processing. However, React still needs the main thread to render. Workers are useful for parsing, sorting, or filtering large datasets before sending results to React state.

items.question: How do I measure INP in local development?
items.answer: Chrome DevTools shows INP in the Performance panel under Web Vitals. The `web-vitals` library reports INP via its callback. For CI, use Lighthouse with `--only-categories=performance` and check the INP metric.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: INP measures worst-case interaction latency, not just first paint
Find long tasks in Chrome Performance panel; correlate with React Profiler
Virtualize long lists, debounce filters, and defer third-party scripts
Test on real hardware with CPU throttling—fast dev machines hide INP problems
data.takeaway: INP debugging is root-cause analysis: find the long task, find the React component, and break the work up.
